top_choice_rationale: P002 (Autor, Hanson, Katz) recognises empirical evidence on how technology and trade shift labour demand, wage structure and local labour-market adjustment. It answers one question with transparent, contestable designs that have been replicated and challenged for more than a decade, and the core work is mature (early 1990s to 2010s). The citation can be worded around the established findings, namely the direction, concentration and persistence of adjustment, and not around the China-shock magnitudes or the whole task framework, which leaves room for the Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane priority. The main costs are real: Dorn is excluded under the three-name cap, the one-versus-two-discoveries boundary is a judgement, and shift-share identification is debated. I rank P001 (Helpman, Melitz) a close second on merit. It has a single originating model, over twenty years of firm-level confirmation, and a distinct advance on the 2008 recognition. Its costs are the uncredited empirical originators and model-dependent welfare magnitudes. Either is preferable to no award, so P000 is last. Support counts are not evidence of merit, though P001 has six explicit supporters and P002 five.
recusal_note: No documented connection to Autor, Hanson, Katz (P002) or to Helpman, Melitz (P001) appears in my profile. Per Krusell (secretary) and John Hassler (chair) are IIES colleagues and frequent co-authors, and both back P001. Peter Klenow is a long-running co-author, but he is credited only on B047, which is in neither proposal. My research on growth, structural change and firm dynamics is adjacent to B044, and I treat that as a reason for caution, not as evidence of merit. Conflicts are disclosed but not adjudicated, and the ballot is completed.
